evidence: src/warehouse/tracking/dtos/create-delivery.dto.ts: CreateDeliveryDto declares @IsString() orderId, truckId, targetPickUpPoint as required strings.
src/warehouse/tracking/dtos/update-delivery.dto.ts: UpdateDeliveryDto declares the same three fields again with their own @IsString() decorators instead of deriving from CreateDeliveryDto.

src/warehouse/tracking/dtos/update-delivery.dto.ts: orderId?, truckId? and targetPickUpPoint? are optional types but have no @IsOptional(), so the copied validation contradicts the intended partial-update behaviour.
Both files serve one concern (delivery input contracts) and use the same validation library, so the problem is duplication, not mixed concerns.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: Both files deal with one concern: input contracts for creating and updating a delivery in warehouse tracking. Both use class-validator in the same way. However, UpdateDeliveryDto re-declares every field of CreateDeliveryDto (orderId, truckId, targetPickUpPoint) along with its validation rule, instead of deriving from it (for example with PartialType(CreateDeliveryDto) plus an id field). So the validation rules for delivery fields live in two places. The copies have already drifted apart: in update-delivery.dto.ts the fields are typed as optional ('?') but still carry a bare @IsString() with no @IsOptional(). class-validator will therefore reject an update that leaves out any of those fields, which contradicts the declared optional types. Copying a rule that should live in one place, with the copies now disagreeing, meets the rubric's failure condition. Confidence is moderate because repeating fields across small DTOs is common practice.
